headline: Spectacle Island Rip Turns On Bass and Blues as Mackerel Show at the Reserved Channel
subhead: The full moon tightened the bunker schools like we said it would, and the harbor islands are the first place to cash in before the North Shore rocks take over.
body_markdown:
This week the call is the harbor islands first, North Shore second, and Plymouth on the back burner until the water cools another few degrees. That's not a knock on Duxbury or Scituate — it's just that the bait is stacking inside the islands right now, and stripers don't leave a buffet to go looking for scraps.

The full moon that came through the night of the 6th did exactly what we flagged it would do — it tightened the bunker schools that have been loose and scattered through the harbor and Broad Sound all August. Peanut bunker and adult menhaden are now balled up tight around Spectacle Island, Long Island Head, and the flats off Deer Island, and the bass have gone from picking at stragglers to actually committing. That's the difference between a flat afternoon and a real bite window, and this week gave us the first taste of the latter.

Tide-wise, the outgoing has been the money stage all week. Current pulls bait off the Deer Island flats and funnels it down through the Gut and past Long Island, and that's where the bass are stacking — 15 to 25 feet of water, current seam visible on the surface, gulls working overhead more mornings than not. Live mackerel on a fish-finder rig, or a chunk of fresh bunker on a 5/0 circle hook, has been the most consistent producer, but topwater guys throwing Doc-style poppers and Danny plugs into the surface wash at first light have had some of the better fish of the week — bass to 34 inches around Spectacle Island's north end on the last two hours of the ebb.

Bluefish are riding shotgun on the same bait and they're not shy about it. Choppers from 3 to 6 pounds have been shredding bunker slicks off Nut Island and inside President Roads, and if you want steady action over quality, a wire leader and a Kastmaster or Hopkins jig worked through the slick will get bit almost every cast during the peak of a feed. The blues are aggressive right now, and they should stay that way into fall — they don't get fussy the way bass sometimes do once the bait balls up tight.

Mackerel showed up in numbers this week off the Reserved Channel and around the Boston Light approach, which is right on schedule and usually the first real sign that the seasonal gears are shifting. Diamond jigs, size 1 to 2, tin-side up, worked with a quick snap-drop retrieve in 20 to 40 feet, are filling coolers fast for anyone who wants fresh bait or a meal. That mackerel push also tells you groundfish season prep is starting — boats working out toward Stellwagen have been marking bait balling up on the structure, and cod and haddock will start staging heavier out there as water temps keep sliding through September.

Up on the North Shore, Nahant and Egg Rock are holding bass but it's been a mixed bag rather than a sure thing. The rocky structure there fishes best on the last two hours of the incoming when water floods over the ledges and pushes bait tight to shore — a white or bone bucktail, 1 to 1.5 ounces, bounced along the boulder fields has taken fish to 30 inches, but the bite has been more about being in the right spot at the right tide stage than blanket numbers. Cape Ann — Halibut Point, Rockport, and around Eastern Point in Gloucester — is fishing similarly: rocky points holding bass on the strong current stages, but you need to be there when the tide's moving, not soaking in the slack.

Flounder fishing inside the harbor has been steady if unspectacular — Dorchester Bay and the channels off Nut Island are giving up flounder in the 12 to 14 inch range on squid strips and sandworms fished on the bottom, a decent option if the bass and blues aren't cooperating on a given tide.

Looking ahead, the pattern that's setting up is the one we've been pointing to for weeks — bunker density in the harbor keeps building, the moon phase keeps working in our favor, and nighttime temps are starting to ease off, which is the last ingredient needed for the first real blitz behavior of the fall. If the wind stays out of the northwest and holds under 15 knots through the weekend, look for the outgoing tide window at Spectacle Island and Deer Island flats to be the highest-odds play — surface activity should build through the week as bait gets pushed harder by the tide range coming off this moon. If you can only get out once, target that morning ebb with a mackerel or fresh bunker chunk and be ready to switch to topwater the second you see birds working. The North Shore rock game will hold through the month as bass filter along the shoreline chasing the same bait south, so there's no rush there — but the harbor islands are the place to be right now while the bunker's still balled up tight.
